opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's one of the things that genuinely surprised us. When you give Genie 3 a prompted world event, say, "a herd of deer runs across the path" or "it starts raining," you might expect it to just inject that immediately, almost like a cut in a film. But often it doesn't. The model seems to find a moment where the event makes sense within the scene that's already unfolding.

For example, if you're walking through a forest and you ask for an animal to appear, it might not pop into the center of the frame right away. It may come in from the edge, from behind a tree, or from somewhere off-screen, so it feels like it was always part of that world. We didn't explicitly program that behavior. There's no rule saying "wait for a plausible entry point." It emerges from training on a huge amount of video, where things in the real world don't just teleport into existence. They arrive in a way that's physically and narratively coherent.

What I find interesting is that this hints at the model having some implicit sense of continuity and causality. It's trying to keep the world consistent with what came before, and the event has to fit that, not override it. It's not perfect. Sometimes the timing is off, or the event takes longer to show up than you'd want, and controllability is definitely something we're still working on. But the fact that it balances following the instruction with keeping the world believable is, to me, one of the more exciting signs that these world models are learning something deeper than pixel prediction.

r001.rationale: The response says Genie 3 often does not inject a prompted event immediately and instead finds a moment when it fits the unfolding scene, clearly indicating that it chooses the timing.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is one of the things that surprised us, honestly. When we talk about promptable world events in Genie 3, the idea is that you're navigating a world with your controller, and then at some point you can type a text prompt like "a herd of deer runs across the field" or "it starts raining," and the model has to figure out how to inject that into the world. And the interesting part is that we don't give the model a hard-coded moment where the event has to happen. It's not like a game engine where you trigger a scripted event on a specific frame.

What actually happens is the model is conditioned on the text, and then it decides, frame by frame, how and when that event should unfold in a way that's consistent with everything it has already generated. So if you ask for deer to appear, the model has to reason, implicitly, about where they could plausibly come from. Maybe there's a tree line to the left, so they emerge from there over the next second or two rather than just popping into existence in the middle of the frame. And that timing emerges from the model's learned sense of what's physically and visually coherent, not from any rule we wrote.

I find that fascinating because it tells you something about what the model has internalized. It has a notion of causality and continuity that's strong enough that it sort of "waits" for the right moment, or finds the right path, to make the event happen. Sometimes it's slightly delayed from what you'd expect, and when you look at why, it's usually because the model needed a few frames to set up the conditions for the event to make sense. The flip side is that it's not always perfectly controllable. There's a tension between responsiveness, which is what you want for interactivity, and plausibility, which is what makes the world feel real. And watching the model negotiate that trade-off on its own is, to me, one of the most interesting behaviors in the system.

r001.rationale: The response says there is no hard-coded trigger time and that the model decides frame by frame when the prompted event unfolds.

astra-6.text: What I find interesting is that the model has to decide not just what the event looks like, but when it makes sense for it to happen. A prompt doesn’t necessarily imply that everything should happen immediately. The timing has to fit the situation and what the user is doing. That makes it a question of how the world unfolds over time, rather than simply whether the model can render the thing you asked for.

r001.rationale: The response says the model decides when an event makes sense to happen and that a prompt does not mean it must happen immediately, clearly conveying that Genie 3 chooses its own timing.

sol-6.1.text: What I find interesting is that the prompt can specify what should happen without specifying exactly when it should happen. So the model has to make that decision in the context of the world and what the user is doing. If you prompt an event, it doesn’t necessarily just happen immediately; there’s a question of finding an appropriate moment. That makes it feel less like a visual effect applied to a frame and more like something unfolding within the world.

r001.rationale: The response says the prompt may leave timing unspecified and that the model chooses an appropriate moment based on the world and user activity.
